# Getting Started

::: {.callout-note title="Learning Goals" collapse="false"}
After this lesson, you should be able to:

* Explain the typical characteristics of a time series
* Explain the typical characteristics of a repeated measures dataset
:::

This brief chapter introduces two different approaches to thinking about
temporal data, as well as two datasets that exemplify each approach.


## Types of Temporal Data

In datasets collected over time, it's useful to think of each observation as a
combination of a collection time and a subject. For example, researchers from
the [Santa Cruz Puma Project][puma] use GPS collars to track the movements of
pumas around Santa Cruz and the San Francisco Bay. Each observation in the
dataset is at a specific time and for a specific puma.

[puma]: https://www.santacruzpumas.org/

<!--
Two kinds of statistical analyses are strongly associated with temporal data:
**time series** and **longitudinal data** analysis.
-->

A **time series** is a dataset where there are lots of observations over time
for each subject. The number of subjects is usually modest---perhaps even just
one. As a consequence, time series analysis methods focus on the observed
subjects rather than the population at large. Major goals include:

* Decomposing the trajectories of individual subjects over time into meaningful
  components; often these are a long-term **trend** component and one or more
  fixed-period **seasonal** components;
* Making predictions or **forecasts** about future measurements.

In contrast, a **longitudinal** (or **repeated measures**) dataset is one where
there are lots of subjects, with a few observations over time for each one. The
number of time points is usually small; there might only be two or three.
Longitudinal data analysis methods tend to focus on the population rather than
the observed subjects. The major goal is typically inference about the
relationship between some predictors and outcome.

We can, of course, apply methods from time series analysis to a longitudinal
dataset and vice-versa. However, making reliable inferences and predictions
about an individual subject's trajectory generally requires lots of
observations of that subject. Likewise, making reliable inferences about a
population generally requires a large sample of subjects.

We distinguish between time series and longitudinal datasets because the
analysis goals and methods are different. We present each separately over the
next two chapters. Nevertheless, there is some overlap, which we'll try to
point out.


## Dataset: Sacramento River Water Temperature {#sec-dataset-sac-water-temp}

The California Department of Water Resources (DWR) monitors water conditions at
multiple stations along the Sacramento River (as well as other waterways in
California). One such station is at [Hood, CA][hood].

[hood]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hood,_California

The DWR publishes most of the data it collects to the [California Data Exchange
Center][cdec]. The examples in this and subsequent chapters use
minimally-cleaned version of the hourly water temperature data collected at the
Hood monitoring station from 2010-2024.

[cdec]: https://cdec.water.ca.gov/

:::{.callout-important}
[Click here][ca-water-temp] to download the 2010-2024 Sacramento River Water
Temperature dataset.

[ca-water-temp]: https://ucdavis.box.com/s/gfgn3vdc8df62uk58338evrdddcgogg7

If you haven't already, we recommend you create a directory for this workshop.
In your workshop directory, create a `data/` subdirectory. Download and save
the dataset in the `data/` subdirectory.
:::

:::{.callout-note
  title="Documentation for 2010-2024 Sacramento River Water Temperature
  Dataset" collapse=false
}

Each row in the dataset contains measurements for one time.

| Column | Description
| -----: | :----------
| time   | Datetime the temperature was collected
| temp_f | Water temperature in degrees Fahrenheit

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25, 75]"}

The source dataset (which is almost identical) is available
[here][ca-water-temp-source] by searching for station ID `SRH`, sensor number
`25`, start date `2010-01-01`, and end date `2024-12-31`.

[ca-water-temp-source]: https://cdec.water.ca.gov/dynamicapp/wsSensorData
:::

After downloading the dataset, we can read it into R with `readRDS`:

```{r}
hood = readRDS("data/2010-2024_sacramento_river_hood_water_temp.rds")
str(hood)
```

This is an example of a time series.


## Dataset: Orange Tree Growth {#sec-dataset-orange}

R's built-in `Orange` dataset records the circumferences of the trunks of five
orange trees, each measured seven times over the course of about 4 years.

:::{.callout-important}
The dataset is included with R as the `Orange` variable.
:::

:::{.callout-note
  title="Orange Tree Growth Dataset" collapse=false
}

Each row in the dataset contains measurements for one tree at one time.

| Column        | Description
| ------------: | :----------
| Tree          | Unique ID number for the tree
| age           | Age of the tree when the measurement was taken, in days since Dec 13, 1968
| circumference | Circumference of the tree in millimeters

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25, 75]"}
:::

This dataset is built into R. We'll use a data-frame-only version (which drops
some additional metadata attached to the dataset):

```{r}
orange = data.frame(Orange)
str(orange)
```

This is an example of a repeated measures dataset.
